process.label: Our process
process.heading: How we work
process.description: Most projects run through the same four steps. You will have something real to click within the first week, and you will never have to guess what happens next.

steps.label: Listen
steps.title: Understand the need
steps.description: We talk about how the business actually runs, what customers ask you for most, and where the current site or process gets in the way. No forms, no discovery questionnaire.
steps.role: One conversation, in person or online.
steps.caption: CG Online Academy, the site as we first saw it

steps.label: Build
steps.title: Build a working demo
steps.description: We build a real, clickable version using your actual content, not a wireframe and not a flat mockup. You see your own business on screen before you have committed to anything.
steps.role: Nothing at all. We come back to you when it is ready.
steps.caption: The working demo from our first meeting

steps.label: Refine
steps.title: You see it, then we refine
steps.description: You click through it, show it to whoever else needs to weigh in, and tell us what is wrong. We adjust and send it back. Two or three rounds is usually enough.
steps.role: Your honest reaction, plus any photos or text only you have.
steps.caption: Lesson pages shaped by client feedback

steps.label: Ship
steps.title: Ship and keep improving
steps.description: We handle the domain, the hosting, the analytics and the handover. After launch we stay on to maintain it and keep adding to it as the business changes.
steps.role: Approve the launch. We take care of the rest.
steps.caption: A client dashboard, live and growing

about.label: About us
about.heading: Small studio. No shortcuts
about.name: Kai Itokazu
about.portraitAlt: Kai Itokazu, founder of Bonsai Digital
about.paragraph1: I am Kai. I grew up in the US, I live in Tokyo, and I have spent my career as an engineer at Meta, Bosch, and Toyota. Bonsai Digital is the studio I run, building websites, web applications, internal tools, and AI agents for businesses here.
about.paragraph2: Engineering is the part most studios leave until last. System design, clean architecture and security are where I start, because a site that looks right but falls over in real use has not actually solved anything.
about.paragraph3: You work with me directly. No account managers, no ticket queues, and we can do all of it in Japanese or English.
about.story: A lot of good businesses in Tokyo are running on a site somebody built ten years ago, or on nothing at all. That is a solvable problem, and fixing it changes how a business gets seen before anyone walks through the door. So I usually build the site first and bring it to the meeting, because it is easier to talk about something you can actually click.

values.title: Speed
values.description: Usually there is a working demo within a week. Often I build it before we even meet, so the first conversation is about something real instead of a proposal.

values.title: Built from scratch
values.description: No templates and no page builders. Everything is written for your business, which makes it quicker to load, safer to run, and possible to change later without starting over.

values.title: Made for real users
values.description: The people using it are usually not technical, and often on a phone in a hurry. It gets designed for them and tested on real devices, not just in a browser on my desk.

definex.title: DefineX
definex.description: A platform that teaches athletes in Japan English, providing all the resources they need to play abroad.
definex.overview: DefineX is a platform dedicated to helping Japanese athletes build English skills. It offers structured courses, learning resources, and ongoing support so athletes have everything they need to pursue opportunities overseas. We partnered with DefineX to build a digital presence that matches their ambitious mission.

showcase.title: Landing Page Redesign
showcase.description: Crafted a modern, conversion-focused landing page that communicates DefineX's mission clearly to athletes and parents.

showcase.title: Academy Page Development
showcase.description: Built a comprehensive academy section showcasing courses, instructors, and learning paths for athletes at every level.

showcase.title: Payment Integration
showcase.description: Implemented secure payment processing with tiered pricing plans for course enrollments and subscriptions.

showcase.title: Email Contact System
showcase.description: Set up a reliable contact system for inquiries, free trial requests, and automated communications.

cgOnlineAcademy.title: CG Online Academy
cgOnlineAcademy.description: A full redesign of a professional 3D artist's online presence, complete with live Three.js model rendering and an integrated course platform with video lessons and progress tracking.
cgOnlineAcademy.overview: CG Online Academy is the revamped digital home for a professional 3D artist and educator. The old site lacked the visual impact needed to reflect the quality of the work being taught. We rebuilt it from the ground up with a modern UI, interactive Three.js model rendering that brings the artist's characters to life in the browser, and a full course platform where students can purchase and follow video lessons with step-by-step guides. Progress tracking keeps everyone on track.

transformation.heading: The Transformation
transformation.description: The client came to us with a website that no longer represented their skill level. The old site was outdated, hard to navigate, and wasn't converting visitors into students. We started by auditing what wasn't working, then rebuilt every page from scratch while keeping the brand identity intact.

showcase.title: Complete UI/UX Redesign
showcase.description: Transformed the CG Online website from scratch. Modernized the visual language, improved information hierarchy, and built a fluid, responsive layout that reflects the quality of the artist's work.

showcase.title: Live 3D Model Viewer with Three.js
showcase.description: Integrated Three.js to render the artist's actual 3D character models directly in the browser. Visitors can interact with real-time rendered models, showcasing the depth of the artist's craft in a way static images never could.

showcase.title: Course Platform with Progress Tracking
showcase.description: Built a full course system where students who purchase a course can access video lessons and written guides directly on the site. Progress is saved per user so they can pick up exactly where they left off.

showcase.title: Student Work Gallery
showcase.description: Dedicated gallery showcasing work produced by students following the courses. It acts as social proof and demonstrates the real-world results of the curriculum.

chnl301.title: Chnl301
chnl301.description: A band website built to give Chnl301 a proper home on the internet, one that captures their sound, their aesthetic, and their story.
chnl301.overview: Chnl301 came to us with a clear vision: they wanted a website that didn't just list their music, but actually felt like them. The brief was to build something with a specific theme and atmosphere that fans would recognize as unmistakably Chnl301. We took that direction seriously, designing and developing every element of the site around their identity, from the visual language and layout to the way their content is presented.

showcase.title: Landing Page & Visual Identity
showcase.description: Designed a landing page that immediately communicates the band's character. From the typography and colour palette to the layout and imagery, every decision was driven by the band's aesthetic direction.

showcase.title: Music & Video Section
showcase.description: Built a dedicated space for the band's music and video content, giving fans an easy way to discover and explore their releases without leaving the site.

showcase.title: Artist Profiles
showcase.description: Each member of the band gets their own spotlight, introducing the people behind the music and deepening the connection between the band and their audience.

homeHairCoffee.title: Home Hair & Coffee Roaster
homeHairCoffee.description: A website for Home Hair & Coffee Roaster, a hair salon and coffee roasting shop in Sanuki, Kagawa.
homeHairCoffee.overview: Home Hair & Coffee Roaster is a unique dual-concept shop in Shido, Sanuki, Kagawa. One side is a relaxed hair salon, the other is a small-batch coffee roasting operation called ARMS Coffee. They needed a site that could present both sides of the business clearly without one overshadowing the other. We designed and built a bilingual website that gives each side its own space while keeping the whole thing feeling cohesive and welcoming.

showcase.title: Hair Salon Section
showcase.description: A clean layout presenting the salon's menu, pricing, and a photography grid that captures the atmosphere of the space. The design keeps things simple and approachable, letting the work speak for itself.

showcase.title: ARMS Coffee Section
showcase.description: A dedicated section for the coffee roasting side of the business, telling the story behind ARMS Coffee with a photo gallery showcasing the beans, the process, and the shop itself.

showcase.title: Shop Info & Contact
showcase.description: All the essential details in one place: location, hours, access, and contact info. Features an illustrated portrait of the owner that adds a personal, handcrafted touch to the page.

influencerAgency.title: Influencer Agency Platform
influencerAgency.description: Automated workflows, a live dashboard, and an AI matching system for Uncharted Influencer Agency, a seven figure agency managing hundreds of creators from a single Google Sheet.
influencerAgency.overview: Uncharted Influencer Agency manages hundreds of creators who together generate millions in campaign revenue, and for years the entire operation ran out of one Google Sheet. The problem is that influencer data never sits still. Follower counts move, average views shift, and contact details go stale. The team wanted to keep the sheet as their source of truth, so we met them where they were. The first phase was a set of automations that update the sheet directly through APIs, with AI enrichment layered on top to capture the qualitative side of each creator. From there we built a dashboard that syncs with the sheet automatically, vectorizes the roster, and runs an AI matching system that suggests the best creators for any campaign brief.

showcase.title: Automations on Top of Google Sheets
showcase.description: The team trusted their spreadsheet and wanted to keep it, so the first phase worked entirely inside it. Scheduled jobs pull fresh follower counts and average views through platform APIs and write them straight back into the sheet, keeping hundreds of rows current without anyone touching a cell.

showcase.title: AI Enrichment for Every Creator
showcase.description: Raw numbers only tell half the story. An AI pipeline reviews each creator and adds qualitative context like content style and niche fit, and it also reads the contact details in their bio to judge which email is actually the right one to reach them at.

showcase.title: A Live Creator Directory
showcase.description: The dashboard syncs automatically with the Google Sheet, which stays the source of truth. Hundreds of creators become a searchable directory with tiers, niches, audience breakdowns, and rates, refreshed every night with no manual data entry.

showcase.title: AI Campaign Matching
showcase.description: The whole roster is vectorized so the platform can run retrieval over it. Drop in a campaign brief and the matching system ranks the creators that fit best, each with a transparent score breakdown across audience, average views, tier, rates, and content fit.

publicSectorAI.title: Public-sector AI platform
publicSectorAI.description: An internal AI and data platform for a public-sector organization: a document assistant that only answers from official sources, analytics dashboards, and automated weekly reporting. Client name kept confidential.
publicSectorAI.overview: This client is a public-sector organization whose name we keep confidential. Their institutional knowledge lived in PDFs, and their reporting was scattered across systems and manual work. We built an internal RAG platform where staff upload PDFs and ask questions in plain language. Every answer is generated strictly from the uploaded documents, and when the documents do not contain the answer, the assistant says so instead of guessing. That design keeps hallucinations out of official work. Around it, we migrated their legacy data into a clean database, built Power BI dashboards and data analysis on top, and set up email automations that run SQL queries on a schedule and deliver weekly reports without anyone lifting a finger.

showcase.title: An Assistant That Knows Their Documents
showcase.description: Staff upload PDFs and ask questions in everyday language, getting answers in seconds instead of digging through files. An admin panel lets the team create assistants per topic, keep them updated, and control exactly who sees what.

showcase.title: Grounded Answers, No Hallucinations
showcase.description: Uploaded documents are indexed into a vector database, and every answer is generated only from the passages retrieved from them. If the documents do not contain the answer, the assistant says so rather than making something up, and sources stay visible so staff can verify everything.

showcase.title: Dashboards and Data Analysis
showcase.description: We migrated scattered legacy data into a clean database, then built Power BI dashboards and analysis on top. Monthly snapshots, year over year trends, and breakdowns that used to take manual spreadsheet work are now a few clicks.

showcase.title: Weekly Reports That Send Themselves
showcase.description: Scheduled automations run SQL queries and email the results out every week. Each report can be toggled, scheduled, and pointed at the right recipients, so recurring reporting no longer takes up anyone's time.

ecommerceOps.title: E-commerce Operations Platform
ecommerceOps.description: An operations console for a retailer selling aftermarket car parts online and through trade workshops. Orders, pre-order deposits, inbound freight, stock and workshop bays sit in one place instead of six separate sheets.
ecommerceOps.overview: The client imports body kit and trim parts from overseas factories and sells to both retail customers and trade workshops. Their whole day ran across a stack of spreadsheets nobody had planned, so we rebuilt it as one console. Orders, pre-orders, suppliers, freight, stock and the workshop calendar all reference each other, and every figure on the dashboard traces back to the rows behind it. The screens here run on stand-in data, with the client's own names, customers and numbers replaced.

problem.heading: The problem
problem.body: The business ran on five or six spreadsheets nobody had planned. One sheet for SKUs and stock counts, another for suppliers and lead times, a third for orders, a deposit tracker for pre-orders, and a freight tab for whatever was still on a boat. None of them referenced each other, so a simple question like “which customer deposits are riding on the container that just slipped two weeks?” meant opening four files and doing the maths by hand. The answer usually arrived after the customer had already called.
problem.artifactAlt: A spreadsheet tracking stock, reorder points and landed cost, with a hardcoded exchange rate and a broken formula
problem.artifactCaption: The stock master this replaced. One hand-typed exchange rate in F2 drives every landed cost on the sheet, the reorder point is blank on some rows, and the deposits customers have paid sit on a different tab that does not link back. Recreated here from the original, with stand-in data.
before: Stock counts and reorder points typed by hand, out of date within a day
Landed cost worked out in a side column against a stale exchange rate
Customer deposits tracked separately from the container they depend on
Workshop bookings on a paper calendar, invisible to whoever answers the phone
after: One record per SKU, with stock, reorder point and landed cost computed together
Every pre-order points at the shipment it is waiting on, so a slipped ETA flags itself
Dashboard figures are clickable, so any number leads back to the rows behind it
Bays, freight and open orders on one screen, in English or Japanese

showcase.title: Deposits tied to the container
showcase.description: A pre-order is money taken against stock that has not landed yet, so it is a liability rather than revenue. Each line points at the inbound shipment it depends on. When a container gets requoted, the customers affected surface straight away instead of a month later.

showcase.title: Stock and landed cost in the same row
showcase.description: 52 SKUs with stock against reorder point, incoming quantities, and the currency working that turns a supplier's foreign price into a real landed cost. Open a row for fitment detail and any pre-orders sitting against it.

showcase.title: Where the money actually comes from
showcase.description: Revenue split by make, category and customer tier, measured against the same window a year earlier. The breakdowns are computed from the order book rather than maintained by hand, so they cannot drift away from the numbers everywhere else.

showcase.title: The same console in Japanese
showcase.description: Every label, status and column has a Japanese counterpart, switched from the header without a reload. For a team in Japan this is not a nice extra, it decides whether the tool gets used at all.

showcase.title: Connected to Shopify
showcase.description: Online sales run through Shopify. Orders flow into the console automatically and are linked to inventory and preorders, so the team never has to keep two systems up to date by hand. From order to arrival to stock on the shelf, the whole chain is visible in one place.

employeeManagement.title: Employee Management Platform
employeeManagement.description: A staffing tool for teams where the same people work on several projects at once. Assign someone on screen, the totals update instantly, and anyone stretched too thin is flagged before it becomes a problem.
employeeManagement.overview: Who is on which project, and in what role? Seventeen people across four projects, all visible in a single table. Allocation totals are calculated automatically, skills are scored so weak spots stand out, and time off shows up in the same view. The client got back the hours they had been spending fixing the workbook, and a plan the whole team could read. The screens here run on stand-in data, with real names and project names replaced.

problem.heading: The problem
problem.body: The team ran staffing out of one shared workbook, and it failed the same way every time. The same person appeared on three tabs with three different percentages. Someone inserted a column and half the totals turned into errors. Skills were recorded as “good” or “needs work”. One person was leaving the team in two weeks, and that fact lived in a cell comment nobody read. The workbook we started from had a change log whose last entry read “not written down anywhere”.
problem.artifactAlt: A staffing spreadsheet with conflicting allocations, a hand-typed total and a broken formula
problem.artifactCaption: The workbook this replaced. One person is at 120% but the total is typed as text, so nothing flags it. Another total broke when someone inserted a column. Nine tabs, and one of them is a copy of the file. Recreated here from the original, with stand-in names.
before: The same person listed on several tabs, each showing a different allocation
Totals typed by hand, with formulas that broke whenever a column was added
Skills written as notes, so nobody could tell which teams were lacking
Departure dates and time off buried in cell comments and email threads
after: No duplicate entries, so allocation totals always add up
Anyone over 100% is flagged right away, not discovered later
Skills scored 1 to 5 per team, so gaps are easy to spot
Every change is saved to an activity log, so nothing gets lost

showcase.title: Capacity at a glance
showcase.description: Headcount, total workload, average utilization and anyone over capacity, shown next to a skill chart for the whole organisation. Open positions and pending time-off requests are on the same screen, so a planning conversation can start and finish in one place.

showcase.title: Skill coverage per team
showcase.description: Select a team to see who's on it, their average experience, and one chart that combines everyone's skill scores. Skills are rated 1 to 5, and any team average below 3.0 is flagged as a gap, so it's clear exactly which role and which skill is missing.

showcase.title: Time off that affects the plan
showcase.description: A monthly calendar color-coded by leave type, with pending requests next to it. Approving a request updates the calendar, the counters and the activity log at once, so time off and staffing are never out of sync.

showcase.title: The same screen in Japanese
showcase.description: Roles, projects, statuses and counters all have Japanese versions, switched from the sidebar. Dates and numbers follow Japanese formatting too, not just translated labels.

enpadel.title: EnPadel
enpadel.description: A bilingual site for a Tokyo padel community built around the idea of 縁, the connections that form through the sport. The hero is a film you scrub by scrolling, with typography timed to the footage.
enpadel.overview: EnPadel runs padel events in Tokyo for a mixed crowd of Japanese players and English-speaking residents, and most of them are meeting the sport for the first time. So the site leads with the feeling rather than the facts. A court film plays as you scroll, five lines of type land in time with it, and only then does the page explain what padel is, who runs it, and when the next event happens. The whole thing is mirrored in Japanese and English, down to the form's subject options.

showcase.title: A film you scroll through
showcase.description: The hero binds scroll position to video playback rather than autoplaying. Three encodes are served depending on what the device can scrub smoothly, and every line of type is placed to avoid the players in frame. Anyone who prefers reduced motion gets a still.

showcase.title: Explaining the sport to newcomers
showcase.description: Most visitors have never played padel, so a dedicated section covers the court, the equipment and how a game runs, using hand-drawn illustrations rather than stock photography. It answers the beginner question without making the brand feel like a beginner brand.

showcase.title: The next event, front and centre
showcase.description: Events are the reason to come back, so the next one gets its own panel with the venue linked to Maps, and past events sit below it with a recap video. When there is nothing scheduled, the section still works as proof that things happen here.

showcase.title: The same site in English
showcase.description: Japanese is the default and English sits at /en, with every string in a single typed dictionary so the two never drift apart. Nav, form labels and subject options all exist in both, which matters for a community that is genuinely half and half.

milleGrass.title: Mille Grass
milleGrass.description: A bilingual site for a fermented set-lunch restaurant in Fujigaoka. One soup and three sides, changing weekly.
milleGrass.overview: Mille Grass serves a weekly-changing fermented set lunch. The site has three jobs: explain what a fermented set lunch is, show the food honestly, and make it easy to check whether the restaurant is open right now. The owner cooks all day, so it also has to be easy to update: the menu is a single photo, and each month's opening days are generated automatically.

showcase.title: A menu the owner can actually update
showcase.description: The paper menu is published as a photo that opens to full size. No dish names or prices live in the code, so updating the menu just means replacing one image. For a restaurant that changes its tray weekly, that keeps the site current without any extra work.

showcase.title: Opening days that generate themselves
showcase.description: The current month's calendar is generated automatically from the opening rules: closed Sunday and Monday, 11:30 to 18:00 on Saturday, 11:30 to 14:30 on weekdays. Nobody has to update it by hand, and visitors can see at a glance whether the restaurant is open today.

showcase.title: The same site in English
showcase.description: The language toggle swaps every string instantly, with no page reload. Fujigaoka has enough non-Japanese residents to make English worth having, and both languages live in one file, so the two versions can't drift apart.

nicolita.title: Nicolita
nicolita.description: A landing site for a Yokohama gelato shop. The flavors change every week, made from local farm produce.
nicolita.overview: Nicolita opens three days a week, and its flavors change weekly based on produce from nearby farms. Until now, all of its information lived on Instagram, which works for regulars but not for first-time visitors. This site covers the essentials: what's available this week, which farm it came from, and clear directions to a store that is genuinely hard to find.

showcase.title: This week's flavours, with the farm named
showcase.description: A carousel of this week's line-up, with each card naming the farm the produce came from. The flavors change every week, so the layout makes that rotation part of the shop's appeal.

showcase.title: Getting people to the door
showcase.description: The shop is six minutes from the station on a street with few landmarks. The visit section brings together the address, hours, parking, payment methods and step-by-step walking directions, with a custom map drawn to match the rest of the page.

showcase.title: The same site in English
showcase.description: The language toggle swaps every string instantly, and the saved preference is read before the page first renders, so returning visitors never see a flash of the wrong language.

arGalleryMVP.title: AR Art Gallery
arGalleryMVP.description: A gallery of public-domain masterworks sold as digital editions, where any piece can be previewed on your own wall in augmented reality before you enquire. Five works, each rendered at the size of the original.
arGalleryMVP.overview: You cannot tell from a thumbnail whether a piece works in your room, or how big it actually is. This MVP answers both before anyone commits: browse the collection on a laptop, open a work on your phone, and place it on a real wall at true scale. Each painting is turned into a textured 3D object at build time, sized from the original's own dimensions, so a portrait work and a landscape one both sit correctly. It went out deliberately small, five works and an enquiry link, so the client could put the idea in front of real users before building a shop around it.

showcase.title: Turn the piece before you place it
showcase.description: Every work loads in an interactive 3D viewer you can drag to orbit. It is the same asset that goes into augmented reality, so what you turn on the desktop is exactly what ends up on the wall. A poster image holds the frame while the model streams in.

showcase.title: Actual size, stated plainly
showcase.description: The placard next to each work gives the edition, the real dimensions, how it mounts and where the original hangs. Scale is the whole argument for previewing in AR, so the number is on the page rather than buried in a spec.

showcase.title: A room, not a grid
showcase.description: The collection is laid out as a gallery wall: gilt frames, a picture light falling across each canvas, museum placards under the work. It reads as somewhere you would buy art rather than a product listing with prices attached.

showcase.title: Each work becomes a 3D object at build time
showcase.description: A build step turns every source image into a textured quad sized from its own aspect ratio, so adding a piece means dropping in a file rather than modelling anything. That is why a portrait like the Vermeer hangs correctly next to a landscape without hand-tuning.

education.label: Education
education.heading: Programming classes for kids
education.description: Alongside our client work, we teach kids how to code. Every lesson is one on one over Zoom, taught in English by the engineer behind Bonsai Digital, who also speaks Japanese.

courses.name: Scratch
courses.description: Scratch is a visual programming language built by MIT for kids. Students snap colorful blocks together to make games and animations, and along the way they pick up the ideas every programmer uses, like loops, conditions, and variables. It feels like play, which is exactly why it works.
learn: Games and animations they can share with friends
The basics: loops, conditions, and variables
How to break a big idea into small steps
A finished project every few lessons

courses.name: Python
courses.description: Python is a real programming language used at companies like Google and Toyota, and it sits at the center of AI. Students write actual code from the very first lesson, building small games and tools while learning to think the way an engineer does.
learn: Real code, written in a real editor
Small games and tools they can actually use
A foundation for AI and more advanced study

education.agesFootnote: Ages are a guide, not a rule. If your child is close in age and curious, the trial lesson is a good place to find the right fit.

items.title: One on one, over Zoom
items.description: Every lesson is private, so it moves at your child's pace. Shy kids get room to ask questions, and quick learners never sit around waiting.

items.title: A real curriculum
items.description: Lessons follow a structured curriculum that builds project by project, so you can see the progress, not just the screen time.

items.title: Taught by a working engineer
items.description: Kids learn from the engineer behind Bonsai Digital, with experience at Meta, Bosch, and Toyota. The habits they pick up are the real ones.

items.title: Taught in English
items.description: Lessons are in English, so kids get real language practice along with the code. The teacher also speaks Japanese, so beginners never get stuck.

cta.heading: The first lesson is free
cta.description: Book a free trial lesson. Your child gives it a try, you see how it all works, and then you decide if it's a good fit.

bookACall.heading: Start your project
bookACall.description: Book a free 30-minute call. We will figure out exactly what you need and the best way to get there.

items.question: How much does a project cost?
items.answer: Every project is different, so we do not publish fixed prices. The best way to get an accurate number is a short call. Most websites start around $1,000 to $4,000 depending on scope. Automations and agent workflows start around $3,000, and full MVP or dashboard builds from $8,000. We have built several of these already, so we can scope them quickly and give you a reliable number on the first call. Larger software and AI systems vary based on complexity.

items.question: How long does it take?
items.answer: A straightforward website typically takes two to four weeks. For MVPs, the whole point is speed, so we aim to get a working first version in front of you and your users within a few weeks. Either way, we usually have something working for you to review within the first week.

items.question: Do I need to be in Japan to work with you?
items.answer: Not at all. We work with clients across Japan and internationally. Everything runs smoothly over video calls and async communication in Japanese or English.

items.question: Can you handle both design and development?
items.answer: Yes, both. We design and build everything ourselves, so there is no coordination overhead between a designer and a developer. You get one person who owns the full picture.

items.question: What happens after launch?
items.answer: We stick around. Everything we build can move onto a monthly maintenance plan covering updates, monitoring, and support. Most clients work with us as a long-term technical partner rather than a one-time vendor.

items.question: Is there a free consultation?
items.answer: Yes. Every engagement starts with a free 30-minute call to understand your situation and figure out the best path forward. No pressure, no obligation.
